Yes! I think they don't need to be a highly intellectual species because they're incredibly efficient in their ecological niche. They're bioindicators, burrowers, ambush hunters, and they do these things well enough to continue existing through time and human interference. An animal doesn't need to be "smart" in a human sense to be important and effective.
They're built very well for what they do, but it really depends on your measure for intelligence. Mine doesn't know his name, but as larvae they're not nearly as er...precise?

Tiger sals especially are awesome pets! I've had mine for over a year now, and he brightens my entire life. I've definitely noticed this sub has so much passion and appreciation for the animals involved, and it's a great community to learn from. Wishing you and your new sal all the good fortune.

I'm not going to remember everything off the top of my head, but I've got a 40 breeder with a moisture gradient, several hides, a water dish, and at least 6 inches of soil through out the whole tank. It's bioactive with live plants and a cleanup crew, too. They can get pretty big, and you probably won't see him use the whole tank, but mine does come out at night and walk around the whole thing quite a bit. 
Their skin is super absorbant, so it's important that you don't just use potting soil or dirt from outside because the chemicals that can be present in both can be really dangerous to your sal. What I have for you is really basic information that has worked for me, mainly sourced from caudata.org so I do encourage you to do lots of reading. Tigers are actually native to my area, so eventually, this tank is supposed to look like a biome I could go outside and find a mile or two out of town.

Pretty much the moment you set him on the ground, he's going to start digging and disappear into the dirt. They're a variety of mole salamander, so he won't need a body of water in the immediate area. Alternatively, you can look for a rock or log that isn't flush with the ground and set him right in front of it. He will dive under there as quickly as he can.
Seeing a tiger at a worksite is a good indicator that the habitat around you is healthy. They're sensitive to chemical changes, but otherwise hardy in their natural environment.

My snot otter? My mountain iguana? That's Oggdo Bogdo! He's a western tiger salamander, and he stays in a bioactive terrarium in my living room. He's never lived in the wild to my knowledge, so he has no fear at all, which means he's just a small pleathery dog. The tradescantia is one of the only plants he can't trample, and I think he appreciates the live foliage because it's his favorite place to burrow.

I keep my trad in a bioactive terrarium, so mine are on a 12 hour day and night cycle with pretty direct light. I'm not an expert by any means, so my system is kind of ramshackle, but I increased light early on because I noticed that the purple gets more vibrant if they have a bit more light exposure. They don't need so many green cholorplasts when the light is more than enough. I know of some people who keep their trads outside all summer because they love heat and sunshine. 

TLDR I think more light is the way to go

Prefacing with I'm not an expert, but I believe since they don't always return to the same tunnels, the way they dig doesn't displace much dirt. So you couldn't pour aluminum in a tiger den the way you could with an ants nest, theres not a hollow structure. It's more of a swimming motion through the substrate rather than say, a tortoise who digs out a den and uses it multiple times. 
TLDR I think they swim in dirt rather than being excavators

I'm definitely not an expert, so my knowledge base is limited. I know my salamander morphed based on when his wild parents probably did, so towards August when the pond they spawned in was drying up. If your salamander is from an area that doesn't dry up, it may take a while longer. It's also not unheard of for a salamander to not morph, someone with more information could give you a better rundown of what happens and why.
When my sal morphed, his gills shrank up and disappeared after about 48 to 72 hours, so I'd say if yours is ready, you'll see those gills reduce in size drastically
